doc.title: Larry Gold interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 18, 2025

title: Scoring animated films from storyboards
summary: Gold describes working from storyboards and dialogue on score paper and learning mag film.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Jazz musicians on film and studio scoring

blocks.x: Yeah. When you did these animated film scores, how do you start? Do you get a synopsis first or do you get sort of a completed animated film?

I always got a storyboard that a lot of times would designate timing. So I would know how long the scene was and sometimes I would get dialogue you know, sometimes you know if the animator would start, we would start with the dialogue. So I would use the dialogue as my — and it was all done with score paper. That was back in the day before computers and it was all done with score paper. And I would write out the dialogue or I'd write out where I wanted things to hit or, you know, and I learned how to, in those days I was always fascinated by the equipment too. I mean I remember — my wife will tell you that in one house I had an 8—track Scully in the basement. You know? I mean I was

always fascinated by the equipment so I learned how to do — what did they call it — Mag film rolls, you know, so that I had you know when you do an animated film you might have the dialogue on one strip and then you have sound effects on another strip, you have music on another strip, and then you have the picture on another strip. And you have control over — hand-cranked — that's the way we did it. So a lot of times I would write to it that way. You know? I would fit the music in — after I wrote it I would — I learned how to use it. I would actually copy it on Mag film and splice it in and if I didn't like some of the things I'd re—splice. I learned how to cut tape in other words.
